feed.title: Yokohama & Fujisawa, Actually
feed.subtitle: Two cities south of Tokyo, written up by someone who lives here. Prices checked, trains timed.

entry.title: Yokohama's Red Brick Christmas market: ¥500 on 27 days, ¥1,000 on 9
entry.summary: Yokohama Red Brick Warehouse Christmas market 2026: which dates cost ¥500 or ¥1,000, what is free without a ticket, an evening's cost, and parking.
entry.content:
The Christmas market at Yokohama Red Brick Warehouse (横浜赤レンガ倉庫) runs until 25 December 2026 and charges for entry: ¥500 on 27 of its 36 days and ¥1,000 on the other 9. This weekend, 28 and 29 November, is the last weekend at ¥500. Every Saturday and Sunday from 5 December costs double.

Two areas beside the market are free, and one of them is on the way in from Sakuragicho Station (桜木町).

I have been to this market. It was too crowded, and I don’t go any more. I also remember wandering around because I couldn’t park the car.

So this piece is for deciding whether you need to go at all, and on which date. Everything else in it comes from the organiser’s pages and three Japanese reports from the opening days, as of 26 November 2026.

The price depends on the date

The organiser sorts the dates into normal days (通常日) and special days (特定日). A normal ticket is ¥500 on a normal day and ¥1,000 on a special day, and the ticket list has no child or student price.

The 9 special days are 5, 6, 12, 13, 18, 19, 20, 24 and 25 December. That is every Saturday and Sunday left after this weekend, plus Friday 18, Thursday 24 and Friday 25 December. Every other day until 25 December is a normal day, which from today leaves 21 days at ¥500.

The market opens at 11:00. It closes at 21:00 until 4 December and at 22:00 from 5 December, with last orders 30 minutes before closing.

Children of elementary-school age and younger enter free all season, with a guardian. Until 4 December, junior-high students are free too. The market’s page does not spell out what a junior-high student pays from 5 December. It lists one price per kind of day.

So 2 adults with 2 elementary-school children pay ¥1,000 on a normal day and ¥2,000 on a special day.

The free day for Yokohama residents was 25 November. It has passed.

At the venue, the ticket is cash only. Same-day normal tickets are sold for cash at the main entrance (メインエントランス), and the ticket site Asoview (アソビュー！) sells them for other kinds of payment. An Asoview ticket does not shorten the wait: by the market’s page, those buyers queue at the normal gate with everyone else.

The priority ticket (優先入場チケット) has its own gate. It costs ¥2,000 on a normal day and ¥2,500 on a special day, and it is sold for a fixed date, in limited numbers, in advance on Asoview only. On either kind of day that is ¥1,500 more than the normal ticket.

A priority ticket that comes with a Noritake mug is ¥4,500 or ¥5,000. That mug is not sold separately.

What is free without a ticket

The market has about 60 food and goods stalls, and entry is charged for the main venue. The organiser lists two more areas, both free to enter.

Christmas Gate is in Shinko Chuo Hiroba (新港中央広場), a square the organiser describes as on the way from the Sakuragicho direction to the warehouse. It has a live tree about 8 m tall from Tokachi in Hokkaido, 18 shops and a children’s corner with a wood-chip sandbox. Payment in this area is cashless only.

Christmas Gate’s page prints two opening times. One section says 16:00 on weekdays until 18 December and 11:00 on weekends and holidays, while the summary on the same page says 11:00 every day.

Iko-yo, a family-outing site that covered opening day, also gives 16:00 on weekdays until 18 December. Plan for 16:00. Christmas Gate closes at 21:05.

Christmas Village is in Aka-Renga Park (赤レンガパーク), next to the main venue. It is open 11:00 to 21:00 until 4 December and 11:00 to 22:00 from 5 December. A Pokémon illumination has been running there since 25 November. One part of it, a tree decorated with the Pokémon you choose, needs a numbered ticket handed out on site from 11:00 each day, one per person.

The main tree is a live Sakhalin spruce (アカエゾマツ) about 11 m tall, with about 20,000 LEDs. It is lit from 16:00 to 23:00, so it stays on for an hour or two after the market shuts. From 16:00 it runs a light show of about 5 minutes every 15 minutes. From 5 December there are no shows from 22:00.

From 4 December, three shows a day, at 17:00, 19:00 and 21:00, are linked to Yorunoyo (ヨルノヨ), the illumination event on Yokohama’s central waterfront. The city’s press release dates Yorunoyo from 4 to 30 December, 17:00 to 21:05.

The organiser’s pages read for this piece do not say whether the main tree can be seen without a ticket, and nobody went to look. Its venue map, a separate booklet, was not read. A local site, Minato to Mirai, describes the way in from the priority gate as heading toward the tree in the centre of the venue.

The two brick buildings are free to walk into. Warehouse 1 (1号館) is open 10:00 to 19:00 and Warehouse 2 (2号館) from 11:00 to 20:00, so both close before the market does.

What an evening costs

Take the Minatomirai Line from Yokohama Station to Bashamichi (馬車道). The fare is ¥200, or ¥193 by IC card, and the warehouse’s access page gives about 6 minutes on foot. Nihon-odori (日本大通り), the next station, is also about 6 minutes on foot and costs ¥230. Use Bashamichi.

The same page gives about 12 minutes on foot from Minatomirai Station (みなとみらい) and about 15 minutes from Kannai (関内) or from Sakuragicho by the Kishamichi promenade (汽車道).

The organiser’s web pages and press release name dishes without prices, and its food booklet was not read for this piece. The prices below come from two Japanese reports, CAKE.TOKYO’s, updated on 24 November, and Iko-yo’s, dated 25 November.

Item Price
Mulled wine (glühwein), red ¥880
Krapfen, a German doughnut, with cinnamon ¥490
A slice of chocolate stollen ¥500
5 sausages with potatoes, at Maruni Wursthaus ¥1,800
Caramel milk tea, at Himmel der Bayern ¥1,100
Holiday Milk Tea or Winter Chai, at the Gogo no Kocha tea stall ¥1,000
Tea churro, at the same stall ¥700

For one adult on a normal day, the train both ways is ¥400, entry ¥500, a mulled wine ¥880 and a Krapfen ¥490. That is ¥2,270. On a special day it is ¥2,770.

I don’t drink alcohol. Swap the wine for a ¥1,000 milk tea and the normal-day total is ¥2,390.

Two adults who each have a mulled wine and share the sausage plate spend ¥5,360 on a normal day, train included.

The market’s own mug costs ¥900, in white or red, with a limit of 2 per person. The food stalls sell it only as a set with a drink. The information desk by the normal gate sells it too.

Inside, the stalls take cash and cashless payment. You cannot top up electronic money on site, and the ATM is on the ground floor of Warehouse 2. Bring cash for the ticket and a card or phone for Christmas Gate.

Food and drink bought elsewhere cannot be brought in. The tables and chairs are outdoors, and the market’s toilets are on the road side of Warehouse 1.

By car: 179 spaces

The warehouse has two car parks, with 83 and 96 spaces. The first hour costs ¥500 and each 30 minutes after that ¥250, so 3 hours is ¥1,500. The access page lists no daily maximum.

For scale, the organiser puts the 2025 market at about 1.21 million visitors, a figure it calculates from visitor numbers at Warehouses 1 and 2.

Spending ¥3,000 in one shop inside the buildings earns 1 hour of free parking. Purchases at the market do not count. The access page excludes outdoor events, and the market’s FAQ excludes shopping in the venue.

The organiser expects congestion at the car parks and on the roads around them on Saturdays, Sundays and holidays, its access page says, and asks visitors to come by public transport. The same page adds that the car parks may be unavailable when full.

For two wheels, the warehouse FAQ puts the bicycle and motorcycle parking beside car park 1, by Warehouse 2. It gives no count and no fee.

Other car parks nearby were not checked for this piece.

What is not good

The queue comes first. The organiser says it may restrict entry when the venue is crowded, and that you may wait to get in however you bought your ticket.

Minato to Mirai’s writer went on opening day, Friday 20 November, and reported about 30 minutes to get in through the normal gate at around 17:30. That was a ¥500 day, on which the market had opened at 17:00. At about 19:00 the same writer found almost nobody at the priority gate, which is in a different place from the normal gate and nearer the stations.

There are no waiting times for the special days here. The organiser charges double on them.

The same writer warns about the sea wind at night, and had trouble finding a place to sit and eat on a weekday night last year. Iko-yo’s advice for the cold is to go into the buildings, which close at 19:00 and 20:00, one to three hours before the market does.

The organiser caps several dishes at 100 or 200 portions a day and one stall’s German white mulled wine at 30 cups a day, its press release says.

The market’s page is silent on re-entry. Assume that leaving means paying again.

English pages are behind. Time Out’s page, dated 27 November 2025, gives ¥500, a 12 m tree and 22:00 closing from 6 December. Tokyo Cheapo’s listing says ¥500 at the door. TripZilla’s 2026 guide, dated 29 September, gives a range of ¥500 to ¥1,000 and says the prices for each date had not been released.

Not checked for this piece: the skating rink the market’s page links to, the organiser’s food booklet and venue map, last trains, and how long the wait is on special days.

Who should go, and when

With children, or on a budget: go by 4 December. This weekend is ¥500, junior-high students are free, and the market shuts at 21:00.

For the lights only: walk in from Sakuragicho by way of Christmas Gate, then go on to Christmas Village. Neither charges entry. From 4 December the main tree’s shows at 17:00, 19:00 and 21:00 are linked to Yorunoyo.

On a special day: buy the ¥2,500 priority ticket in advance, or plan to stand in line at the normal gate.

By car: there are 179 spaces. Take the train.

If an acquaintance visiting from abroad asked me for one place here, I would take them to a small izakaya, a pub that serves food, in Noge (野毛) or around Yokohama Station or Bandobashi (阪東橋). I assume they will go to the Red Brick Warehouse anyway.

entry.title: Nogeyama Zoo closes from 7 January: Yokohama's three zoos, priced
entry.summary: Yokohama's three city zoos compared for families: entry fees, parking, time needed, free Saturdays, and Nogeyama Zoo's closure from 7 January 2027.
entry.content:
Yokohama runs three zoos. Nogeyama Zoo (野毛山動物園) is free, small and a 15-minute walk from Sakuragicho Station (桜木町), and it closes for renewal works from 7 January 2027. The city plans to reopen it in 2029 and has not fixed a date.

Zoorasia (よこはま動物園ズーラシア) is the big one: ¥800 for an adult, and 3 to 4 hours for one lap. Kanazawa Zoo (金沢動物園) is ¥500 and sits on a hill inside a nature park.

So this winter the choice has a deadline. If you want the free zoo, you have until the first days of January. If you have a car and a whole day, go to Zoorasia. If you want half a day with a long slide next door, go to Kanazawa.

With my daughters, the zoo I go to most is Zoorasia. It is 40 minutes from our home. Nogeyama is awkward to reach by car, so we rarely go. Kanazawa is where I sometimes go for a barbecue, and my impression is that it is hillier than the other two.

Everything else here comes from the zoos’ and the city’s own pages, as of 25 November 2026.

The three zoos side by side

The city owns all three and one foundation, Yokohama-shi Midori no Kyokai (横浜市緑の協会), runs them. Their standard hours match: 9:30 to 16:30, with last entry at 16:00. All three are shut from 29 December to 1 January.

Zoorasia Kanazawa Nogeyama
Ward Asahi Kanazawa Nishi
Opened 1999 1982 1951
Area 45.3 ha 12.8 ha 3.3 ha
Adult, 18 and over ¥800 ¥500 Free
High-school student ¥300 ¥300 Free
Elementary or junior-high student ¥200 ¥200 Free
Below elementary-school age Free Free Free
Regular closed day Tuesday Monday Monday
Car park spaces 2,200 1,200 None
Car park fee ¥1,000 ¥600
Stroller hire ¥600 ¥300 Free, 4 only
One lap, by the zoo’s FAQ 3 to 4 hours 1.5 to 2 hours 1 to 1.5 hours

Each lap time excludes breaks and meals. When the closed day falls on a public holiday, the zoo opens that day and closes the next. Kanazawa has no closed days in May and October.

Zoorasia covers 13.7 times the ground Nogeyama does. That one number explains most of the table.

The city’s FAQ counts three zoos and one branch, a 0.2-hectare children’s zoo at Makigahara (万騎が原ちびっこ動物園) in Asahi ward, also free. It was not researched for this piece beyond that line.

Nogeyama: free, and shut from 7 January 2027

Nogeyama Zoo charges nobody. Its notice, updated on 12 June 2026, says the zoo closes for renewal works from 7 January 2027. Reopening is planned for 2029 and, in the notice’s own words, not decided. The rest of Nogeyama Park stays open.

The notice names the first closed day. It does not name the last open one. The zoo’s pages give this much:

  • Monday 28 December to Friday 1 January: closed for the year end.
  • Saturday 2 and Sunday 3 January: a poster-calendar giveaway at the entrance from 9:30, for the first 200 visitors each day. The zoo calls it the last one before the closure.
  • Monday 4 January: a Monday, the regular closed day.
  • Tuesday 5 and Wednesday 6 January: open days by the normal rule.

No page read for this piece confirms 4, 5 or 6 January, and the zoo’s visitor page says it sometimes opens on a closed day. The safe last days are 2 and 3 January.

There is no car park. The entrance has 3 spaces for disabled visitors, which cannot be reserved. On foot the zoo is 15 minutes from Sakuragicho on JR and the Blue Line, and 10 minutes from Hinodecho (日ノ出町) on the Keikyu Line. The zoo’s driving directions end with the words “the zoo is at the top of the slope”.

City bus route 89 runs every day and stops at Nogeyama Dobutsuen-mae (野毛山動物園前), right by the zoo. The Transportation Bureau’s page puts it at platform 1 of the east exit bus terminal at Yokohama Station and platform 8 at Sakuragicho Station. The same page gives about 20 minutes from Yokohama Station.

The fare is ¥220, or ¥110 for a child. Up to 2 children under 6 ride free with each guardian. The city has applied to raise the adult fare to ¥240 in January 2027, and on its page updated on 23 October 2026 the date was still open.

On the way back, read the sign on the bus. Some buses from the zoo stop go through to Yokohama Station and some end at Sakuragicho.

The petting area, Nakayoshi Hiroba (なかよし広場), has guinea pigs and mice. Every session has to be booked in advance on the zoo’s reservation system. Booking opens at 12:00 one week before the day, first come, first served.

There are 7 sessions of 15 minutes each, 3 in the morning from 10:20 and 4 in the afternoon from 13:30. Each takes 10 groups of up to 5 people, and one person can join one session a day. A child of elementary-school age or younger cannot book alone.

English listings lag behind. Time Out’s page on the zoo is dated 8 January 2020 and says “numbered tickets are required” for the petting area. Good Luck Trip’s family list, updated on 14 May 2026, describes Nogeyama without mentioning the closure.

Zoorasia: the one that takes a day

Zoorasia kept about 95 species and 470 animals at the end of March 2026. Every public-transport route on its access page involves a bus.

Buses marked Yokohama Dobutsuen (よこはま動物園) leave the north exits of Tsurugamine (鶴ヶ峰) and Mitsukyo (三ツ境) on the Sotetsu Line and take about 15 minutes. From the south exit of Nakayama (中山), on the JR Yokohama Line and the Green Line subway, the bus takes about 18 minutes. A bus from Yokohama Station takes about 1 hour, and the zoo’s page warns that there are few of them.

The car park holds 2,200 cars and costs ¥1,000 a day. It opens 1 hour before the zoo and shuts 1 hour after it, and stops taking cars 30 minutes before the zoo closes. On Saturdays, Sundays and holidays in November 2026 the zoo is trying out a ¥1,500 fee. Two of those days are left, 28 and 29 November.

Inside, a bus runs direct between the Zou-san stop (ゾウさんのりば) by the main gate and the north gate stop. It costs ¥200 from junior-high age up and ¥100 for elementary-school children, and it is cash only. The north gate itself opens only on weekends, holidays and busy days.

The ticket machines take credit cards, and the entry gates take a transport IC card such as Suica or PASMO. Keep the ticket: showing it lets you back in on the same day.

Kanazawa Zoo: the one on a hill

Kanazawa Zoo takes up 12.8 hectares of Kanazawa Nature Park, which the zoo’s site puts at about 600,000 square metres of hills. It keeps mostly plant-eaters. The city’s FAQ names Indian elephants, giraffes, Indian rhinoceroses and koalas. The zoo counted 51 species and 1,154 animals on 31 March 2026.

There are two car parks, both ¥600, both normally open 9:00 to 17:00 with last entry at 16:30.

The front car park (正面口駐車場) has 450 spaces and is entered from an ordinary road, the Sasage-Kamariya road (笹下釜利谷道路). From there the Koala Bus (コアラバス), a free shuttle, takes about 5 minutes, and the entrance is about 3 minutes further on foot. Walk the whole way and the zoo’s own figure is about 20 minutes for an adult, uphill.

The expressway-side car park (高速側駐車場) has 750 spaces and is about 3 minutes on foot from the entrance. It connects only to the Yokohama-Yokosuka Road (横浜横須賀道路), through a dedicated gate at the left end of the Kamariya toll plaza (釜利谷料金所). You cannot reach it from ordinary roads.

By train, go to Kanazawa-bunko (金沢文庫) on the Keikyu Line and take the west exit to bus stop 1. The Keikyu bus for Nomura Jutaku Center (野村住宅センター) takes about 10 minutes to Natsuyamazaka-ue (夏山坂上), and the entrance is 6 minutes on foot up a gentle slope. On Saturdays, Sundays and holidays an express bus runs direct to the zoo.

The park’s botanical zone, outside the zoo gate, is open 9:00 to 17:00 every day of the year, and the fee page lists a charge only for the zoo. It has a 100 m roller slide.

The barbecue areas are in the botanical zone too, in Nonbiri Nohara (のんびり野原) and part of Nandaro-zaka (なんだろ坂), and are booked through an outside operator’s website. The zoo’s page gives no prices for them. The park’s own description of Nandaro-zaka is a steep slope.

What a family pays

Take 2 adults and 2 children at elementary school.

Saturday Other open days Car park
Zoorasia ¥1,600 ¥2,000 ¥1,000
Kanazawa ¥1,000 ¥1,400 ¥600
Nogeyama ¥0 ¥0 None

Zoorasia’s car park is ¥1,500 on 28 and 29 November.

On Saturdays, elementary, junior-high and high-school students enter both paid zoos free. Zoorasia asks for a student ID. Kanazawa accepts anything that shows the child’s age.

Going to Nogeyama by bus from Yokohama Station and back costs the same family ¥1,320 at today’s fares. Walking from Sakuragicho costs nothing.

The annual pass costs ¥2,000, is sold to visitors aged 18 and over, and is valid for one year from the day of purchase at both paid zoos. Three Zoorasia visits at ¥800 come to ¥2,400, so the pass pays for itself on the third. The fee pages list no pass for anyone under 18.

What is not good

Nogeyama is already emptying. The zoo’s relocation list, updated on 19 October 2026, dates the moves of its Japanese black bears, raccoon dogs and Abyssinian colobus monkeys to Zoorasia between 9 March and 9 November 2026. The relocation list has the condor, ostrich and flamingos going to zoos in Tokushima, Hamamatsu and Saitama Prefecture, with dates from 23 March to 27 April 2026.

The relocation list does not say which moves have been carried out. Check it before you promise a child a bear.

The relocation list also has red pandas and Humboldt penguins going to Zoorasia for the closure, with no dates. Giraffes, Grevy’s zebras and chimpanzees are among the animals it shows staying on the site.

Nogeyama has 4 strollers to lend and no car park. The petting area takes 70 groups a day, and without a booking you do not get a session.

Zoorasia is a bus ride from every station, and the ride from Yokohama Station is about an hour. The in-park bus is a second fare on top of entry. One ride for 2 adults and 2 elementary-school children is ¥600 in cash.

At Kanazawa, a missed Koala Bus from the front car park means a 20-minute climb. Both car parks are shut on the zoo’s closed days, even though the botanical zone is open all year. The expressway-side car park is useless if you came by ordinary roads.

All three stop letting people in at 16:00.

Some things were not checked for this piece: bus fares to Zoorasia and Kanazawa, which are set by other bus companies, how fast the petting sessions fill, and the queues at the gates and car parks. There are no numbers for those here.

Which one, and when

Before 7 January, without a car: Nogeyama. Book the guinea pigs at 12:00 exactly one week ahead. Go before 28 December, or on 2 or 3 January.

With a car and a full day: Zoorasia, on a Saturday if your children are at school. The ¥1,500 parking trial covers 28 and 29 November.

With half a day, or a barbecue booked: Kanazawa. Use the front car park and wait for the Koala Bus.

From 7 January two zoos are left, and the cheaper visit for that family is Kanazawa on a Saturday, at ¥1,000.

entry.title: Enoshima's winter lights start on 1 December: dates, hours and prices
entry.summary: Shonan no Hoseki 2026-27 on Enoshima runs 1 December to 28 February. Lighting hours by date, entry prices after 17:00, and trains from Fujisawa Station.
entry.content:
Enoshima’s winter illumination, Shonan no Hoseki (湘南の宝石), starts on Tuesday 1 December 2026 and runs to Sunday 28 February 2027. Last season it opened on 22 November. If you planned a late-November evening around an older guide, the lights will be off.

The short version: the lights come on at 17:00. The main display is inside a garden at the top of the island, which costs ¥500 from 17:00. Going up the tower in the middle of it is listed as a further ¥800. From Fujisawa Station the train takes 7 minutes and costs ¥170, and then you walk for about 20 minutes.

This piece is desk research. Nobody visited for it. The dates, hours and prices come from three Japanese event listings that carry the organiser’s announcement, and they agree with each other.

The dates, and why older pages are wrong

This is the 27th edition. It was recognised in 2025 as one of Japan’s three great illuminations, which is why it turns up in most winter lists for the Tokyo area.

English lists can be a season behind. One English listing checked for this piece still gives the start as late November. Last season that was right: 22 November 2025 to 28 February 2026. This season the first night is 1 December, nine days later.

The lights are in three places: Enoshima Samuel Cocking Garden (江の島サムエル・コッキング苑) at the top of the island, other spots on the island, and the Katase coast on the mainland side. The listings name two fees, both inside the garden. They do not say whether the island and coast displays cost anything, so that is not stated here either.

Lighting hours change four times

On an ordinary weekday the lights run from 17:00 to 20:00. On Saturdays, Sundays and public holidays they run to 21:00.

From Saturday 19 December to Wednesday 30 December they run to 21:00 every night, weekdays included.

From Thursday 31 December to Sunday 3 January they stop at 20:00 every night, even on the weekend.

From Saturday 16 January the start moves to 17:30, for weekdays and weekends alike.

The listings for this season give no last-entry time. Last season it was 30 minutes before the lights went off: 19:30 on weekdays and 20:30 on weekends. Plan as if that still applies.

What it costs

There are two fees.

Entry to the garden is free until 17:00. From 17:00 it is ¥500 for adults and ¥250 for children.

The Sea Candle is the lighthouse tower inside the garden. Its fee is listed as ¥800 for adults and ¥400 for children. Its viewing floor is 41 metres above the ground and 101 metres above the sea.

The listings show these as two fees for two things. If both are charged in full, an adult who enters the garden and goes up the tower pays ¥1,300. No combined ticket price was confirmed for this piece.

Whether someone who walks into the garden at 16:50 is asked to pay at 17:00 was not confirmed either. Do not build your evening on that.

The train from Fujisawa Station is cheap. The Odakyu Enoshima Line to Katase-Enoshima (片瀬江ノ島) is ¥170 each way, ¥167 with an IC card. So the evening from Fujisawa Station comes to:

Adult
Odakyu, Fujisawa to Katase-Enoshima and back ¥340
Garden entry from 17:00 ¥500
Without the tower ¥840
Sea Candle ¥800
With the tower ¥1,640

Getting there from Fujisawa Station and from Yokohama

Fujisawa Station (藤沢) is the place to change. From Yokohama Station it is 20 minutes on the JR Tokaido Line. From Shonandai it is 7 minutes by Odakyu express and ¥200.

At Fujisawa you choose between two trains.

The Odakyu Enoshima Line takes 7 minutes to Katase-Enoshima and costs ¥170. Katase-Enoshima is the closest station to the island: about 20 minutes on foot to the garden.

The Enoden takes about 10 minutes to Enoshima Station (江ノ島) and costs ¥220. From there the walk to the garden is about 25 minutes. The two stations are 11 minutes apart on foot.

The Shonan Monorail’s Shonan-Enoshima Station is a third way in, about 26 minutes on foot from the garden.

For this trip the Odakyu line is ¥50 cheaper each way and leaves you five minutes closer. Take the Enoden if the Enoden itself is part of what you came for.

Train times and fares above are from route searches. The Fujisawa to Katase-Enoshima fares come from searches dated July to September 2026, and the others from 19 November 2026.

What is not good

It is a 20-minute walk before you see the main display, and it ends in a climb. The tower’s viewing floor is 101 metres above the sea and 41 metres above the ground, which puts the garden about 60 metres up.

On a weekday you have three hours, 17:00 to 20:00. From Shinjuku, the routes checked took between 62 and 112 minutes to Katase-Enoshima. Leave Tokyo after work and a large part of the three hours goes on trains.

The organiser extends the hours every night from 19 to 30 December. That is a fair sign of when the most people are expected. If you can choose, the first two and a half weeks of December and the weeks after mid-January are the other options, and from 16 January you lose the first half hour.

It is an island, in winter, after dark. Nothing in the listings says what happens in bad weather.

The organiser’s own page could not be opened when this piece was checked. Before you travel, confirm the hours and fees on the official Shonan no Hoseki page (Japanese).

If you only remember three things

The first night is 1 December.

Bring ¥500 for the garden, and ¥800 more if you want the tower.

From Fujisawa Station, take the Odakyu line to Katase-Enoshima.

entry.title: The map residents actually use for Yokohama and Fujisawa
entry.summary: A resident's orientation to Yokohama and Fujisawa: population by ward, the three railways linking them, and fares and times checked in November 2026.
entry.content:
Most guides give you two dots. One is Yokohama’s harbour: Minato Mirai, Chinatown, Yamashita Park. The other is Enoshima, the small island off Fujisawa’s beach. Both are worth a day. Together they cover a thin slice of the two cities.

I live in the rest. My home is in Izumi ward, a part of Yokohama I call its countryside. I’m a software engineer and a father of two, and I ride a 125cc Honda Monkey. This site is where I write the two cities down as the people here use them, with the prices and the minutes checked.

This first piece is the map. Learn three railway lines and everything else on the site will fall into place.

Yokohama is 18 wards, and the harbour is two of them

Yokohama had 3,753,462 residents on 1 October 2026, by the city’s own estimate. It is the most populous municipality in Japan. Tokyo is larger, but Tokyo is run as 23 separate wards, each counted on its own.

The city covers 438 square kilometres and is divided into 18 wards (ku, 区). The harbour that visitors photograph sits in two of them, Nishi and Naka. On 1 November 2024 those two wards held about 261,000 people, out of 3.77 million. That is about 7%.

The other 93% live inland and along the railways. Kohoku ward alone had 365,668 residents in July 2026. Most visitors never hear the names of wards like Totsuka, Asahi, Izumi and Seya, and that is where a large part of the city sleeps.

This has a practical consequence. The Yokohama of supermarkets, schools, rents and commutes is the inland one. If you are choosing where to stay for a week or where to live for a year, the harbour tells you little.

Fujisawa is three towns stacked north to south

Fujisawa is smaller: about 445,000 people on the resident register on 1 January 2025. It has been a city since 1940. Enoshima is part of it, which surprises people who assume the island belongs to Kamakura next door.

Think of Fujisawa as three bands.

The south is the coast on Sagami Bay: the beaches of Katase, Kugenuma and Tsujido, and Enoshima. The land here is flat.

The middle is Fujisawa Station (藤沢), where the shops are, and where JR, the Odakyu line and the Enoden meet.

The north is low hills, and its main station is Shonandai (湘南台). Three railways stop there, and two of them end there.

Six railway operators run inside this one city: JR’s Tokaido Main Line, Odakyu, Sotetsu, the Enoden, the Yokohama Municipal Subway and the Shonan Monorail. That much track is the reason Fujisawa works as a base for a whole trip, well beyond one afternoon on the island.

Three lines tie the two cities together

The JR Tokaido Line is the fast one. Fujisawa Station to Yokohama Station takes 20 minutes. Stay inside the JR gates, ride the Negishi Line one more stop, and you are at Sakuragicho (桜木町), the station for the harbour. The JR fare from Fujisawa to Sakuragicho is ¥440.

The Blue Line is Yokohama’s municipal subway. It has 32 stations and runs from Azamino in the north of the city to Shonandai. Its last stop is across the city boundary, in Fujisawa. From Shonandai it reaches Sakuragicho with no change in 37 minutes for ¥370. It is slower than JR, and you never have to think.

The Sotetsu Izumino Line also ends at Shonandai. It reaches Yokohama Station by way of Futamatagawa (二俣川). On the trains checked for this piece, the ride was 11 minutes to Futamatagawa and 16 minutes on from there, and the fare for the whole ride was ¥370.

Inside Fujisawa, the Odakyu Enoshima Line joins the north to the middle. Shonandai to Fujisawa Station is 7 minutes by express and costs ¥200. The same line continues to Katase-Enoshima, the station nearest the island. The Enoden leaves from Fujisawa Station too, and runs along the coast to Kamakura.

Every fare and time above is for a weekday morning, looked up on 19 November 2026. With an IC card such as Suica or PASMO a few of these fares come out ¥1 to ¥7 lower.

Old guides have the wrong JR fares

JR East raised its fares on 14 March 2026. The company described it as its first fare revision since it was created in 1987, and the minimum fare went from ¥150 to ¥160. A JR fare printed in a guide from before that date is wrong.

Every fare on this site carries the date it was checked. When a fare changes, the piece gets corrected and the correction is dated.

What is not good about this map

The lines do not meet where you want them to. Shonandai and Fujisawa Station are both in Fujisawa, and they are 7 minutes and ¥200 apart on a different company’s train.

Japanese railways charge per operator. A trip that uses two companies costs two fares. Shonandai to Sakuragicho is ¥370 on the Blue Line alone. Go by Odakyu and JR through Fujisawa Station and the same trip is ¥640. It took 43 minutes on the morning checked, 6 minutes longer than the subway. The route that looks clever costs ¥270 more and saves no time.

The Blue Line is slow. Those 37 minutes cover 20.4 km, which works out to about 33 km/h.

And this map leaves out buses, which many inland neighbourhoods depend on. No bus fares were checked for this piece, so there are none in it.

How to use it

If you are visiting, choose where you sleep by line. A hotel near Yokohama Station is 20 minutes from Fujisawa Station on JR, and Fujisawa Station is where the Odakyu line and the Enoden leave for Enoshima.

If you are thinking of living here, choose the line first and the ward second. The line decides your commute and your fare. The ward decides which city office you queue at.

Before you compare two routes, count the companies. One company, one fare.

Every piece on this site says which line it is on.
